comparison: Both evaluations support the IRI findings (C17-C22) showing participants plan future reaches in advance. OpenEval provides detailed statistical assessment noting appropriate sample sizes and p-values, while peer reviewers affirm the evidence is 'compelling' without raising methodological concerns. Both agree on the two-targets-ahead planning claim (C22), though OpenEval notes the effect is small and only significant for shortest dwell time.

Both evaluations support the target jump experiment findings (C23-C30). OpenEval emphasizes converging kinematic and temporal evidence with appropriate controls, noting only that multiple comparison corrections should be clarified. Peer reviewers praise the 'clever target jump manipulations' and accept the evidence without methodological concerns. Both agree the experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis.

Both evaluations strongly support the interaction between planning processes (C31-C40). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the experimental logic and statistical evidence (p<0.01), noting the interpretation of shared computational resources (C39) is reasonable though speculative. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm planning processes are 'not independent' and accept the evidence as 'compelling' without raising concerns.

Perfect agreement on ruling out chunking hypothesis (C41-C49). Both evaluations accept the evidence from speed profiles and selective correction patterns. OpenEval notes the logic is sound but suggests the characterization of chunking (C43) could be more precisely defined with citations. Peer reviewers accept the conclusions without challenging the methodology or interpretation.

Both evaluations support the co-articulation findings (C50-C63). OpenEval emphasizes the sophisticated PCA-based curvature analysis and the critical finding that co-articulation only occurs with temporal overlap, noting robust statistical evidence with multiple comparison corrections. Peer reviewers confirm reaches are more efficient in 'timing and path curvature' and accept the temporal overlap requirement without questioning the methodology.

Both evaluations support the eye-tracking findings (C64-C72). OpenEval notes the parafoveal processing inference (C65, C72) is reasonable given the one-saccade-per-reach pattern, though direct evidence would require additional experiments. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the parafoveal acquisition finding without requesting additional experiments, accepting the interpretation as appropriate for the behavioral data.

OpenEval R7 evaluates summary claims C1-C5 as supported, noting C5 is appropriately qualified as speculative. Peer R1 focuses on the empirical IRI findings (C1, C17-C22) and affirms the evidence is compelling. Both support C1, but OpenEval addresses the broader set of summary claims while peer review focuses on the specific IRI data.

OpenEval R7 addresses summary claims including C2-C3 about planning interaction. Peer R3 evaluates the detailed empirical evidence for interaction (C2-C3, C31-C40). Both support the interaction claims, but OpenEval evaluates them as summary statements while peer review evaluates the underlying empirical evidence.

OpenEval R7 includes C4 about co-articulation as part of summary claims evaluation. Peer R5 evaluates the detailed co-articulation evidence (C4, C50-C63). Both support the co-articulation findings, with OpenEval treating it as a summary claim and peer review evaluating the detailed empirical evidence.

OpenEval R7 evaluates C5 about functional significance as appropriately qualified speculation. Peer R7 evaluates broader neural mechanism speculation (C5, C82-C92) as reasonable interpretation and future direction. Both accept C5 as appropriate speculation, though peer review groups it with more extensive neural mechanism discussion.

Perfect agreement on the comparison with Ariani et al. 2021 (C73-C77). Both evaluations accept this as appropriate discussion. OpenEval notes the comparison is qualitative rather than quantitative and the explanations are speculative but reasonable. Peer reviewers accept the comparative discussion without challenge, not requesting additional experiments to resolve differences.

OpenEval R9 evaluates contextualization with Ames et al. 2019 and obligatory interaction conclusion (C78-C82) as supported, noting mechanisms are speculative but reasonable. Peer R7 includes C82 in broader neural mechanism discussion, accepting it as reasonable interpretation. Both support the obligatory interaction conclusion (C82), though OpenEval focuses on literature contextualization while peer review groups it with neural speculation.

OpenEval R10 evaluates neural mechanism speculation (C83-C92) as uncertain but valuable theoretical discussion, appropriately acknowledging need for further experiments. Peer R7 evaluates overlapping neural claims (C83-C84, C88-C92) as supported reasonable interpretation and exciting future direction. OpenEval is more cautious (UNCERTAIN) while peer reviewers are more accepting (SUPPORTED), though both agree the speculation is appropriate.

Both evaluations address the eye-hand dissociation (C93-C96). OpenEval rates it as uncertain, noting the observation is valid but interpretation is highly speculative with alternative explanations not considered. Peer reviewers support it, accepting the observation and interpretation without challenge. OpenEval is more critical of the speculation while peer reviewers accept it as appropriately qualified hypothesis for future work.

OpenEval R12 evaluates methodological details (C13-C16, C97-C113) as supported, noting adequate sample sizes, well-controlled manipulations, and complete documentation supporting reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately evaluate methodological claims.

OpenEval R13 evaluates analysis methods (C114-C122) as supported, praising sophisticated curvature analysis, appropriate exclusion criteria, and proper statistical corrections. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers accepted the analytical approaches without separate evaluation.

OpenEval R14 evaluates introduction and background claims (C6-C12) as supported, noting accurate citations, appropriate description of prior work, and clear identification of knowledge gap. No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately evaluate introduction claims.
